channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: France will bring forward a 1.6% rise in the minimum wage from January 2027 to December 2026, Prime Minister Lecornu announced on 9 November to defuse a cost-of-living crisis, a smaller rise than the unions demanded.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that on 9 November Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced that a planned rise in the national minimum wage will be brought forward from January 2027 to December 2026, to defuse a cost-of-living crisis that has led to some of France's worst civil unrest in years. It gives the rise as 1.6%, which brings the monthly minimum wage to a net EUR 1,502, up EUR 24 from the level in force since June 2026, when it was raised by EUR 35. Handelsblatt, citing Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou, gives the same 1.6% rise and a monthly minimum of about EUR 1,867 rising to about EUR 1,897, nearly EUR 30 more on a 35-hour week; the row does not say whether those figures are gross or net. Handelsblatt adds that the government will also raise a number of subsidies and aid measures. The CFDT, France's largest union, had called for a rise of EUR 100 and the left-wing CGT for 10%, around EUR 150 a month. The rows do not give the cost to employers or the list of the other aid measures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a government decision that lifts a labour cost floor earlier than planned. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a minimum wage rise of 1.6% raises labour costs most in low-wage sectors and can feed into wage negotiations above the minimum. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, French customers in construction, furniture and packaging have labour-intensive operations, so higher minimum wages add to their costs; the rows give no sector figures. Points that may be worth considering include the unions' reaction, the 2027 budget and the next inflation data.

MarketScreener | Handelsblatt

item.title: China's foreign trade surplus reached about USD 1.04 trillion as of October 2026, with October imports up 41.6% and exports up 35.2% from a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data reported by Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
item.description:
Sueddeutsche Zeitung reports, citing the Chinese Customs Administration, that China's foreign trade surplus in US dollars reached about USD 1.04 trillion as of October 2026. In October, imports grew 41.6% and exports 35.2% from a year earlier. Imports from Africa, Southeast Asia and the US grew by between 35% and 42%, while imports from Germany fell 2.6%; exports to Germany rose 33.5%. The row does not say whether the surplus covers the year to date or a twelve-month period, whether the country figures cover October or the year to date, or which products drive exports, and it gives no figure for the value of exports or imports. It is the only row in the input with these figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives national totals and a few country figures, not products or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a surplus of this size and exports to Germany growing much faster than imports from Germany add to import competition in Europe and tend to bring pressure for trade-defence measures and for exchange-rate adjustment. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher Chinese exports of finished goods and intermediates can lower prices in customer industries such as machinery and vehicles, and a 41.6% rise in China's October imports may reflect demand for inputs there; the row gives no figures for chemicals trade. Points that may be worth considering include the product breakdown in the customs release and the November data.

Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Commissioner Dombrovskis says the EU wants to cover about EUR 45 billion of the extra EUR 70 billion Ukraine needs, and Chancellor Merz says he will block the EU's 2028-2034 budget unless all member states commit to funding Ukraine in 2027 and beyond.
item.description:
Wallstreet:online reports that EU Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting with the member states' finance ministers in Brussels, said Ukraine needs an additional EUR 70 billion, of which the EU wants to cover around two-thirds, about EUR 45 billion. The row says the EU approved EUR 90 billion for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027 last year and that President Zelenskyy demanded the extra EUR 70 billion in October for the coming year. The Financial Times reports that Merz has warned in a letter to European Council President Antonio Costa that he will block the EU's next seven-year budget, for 2028-2034, unless all EU countries agree to fund Ukraine in 2027 and beyond; the FT describes a EUR 70 billion financing gap next year. The rows do not say which countries have declined to commit, what the extra funding would be paid from or when decisions are due.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a funding intention and a condition set by one government, not a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a veto threat over the multi-year budget links the Ukraine funding question to all other EU spending lines and delays decisions on both. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, EU budget lines support infrastructure, energy and industrial programmes that affect construction and manufacturing demand, and the budget's size and timing set the funding available for them; the rows give no figures for those programmes. Points that may be worth considering include the reactions of other member states to the letter, the next finance ministers' and leaders' meetings and the Commission's formal proposal.

Wallstreet:online | The Financial Times

item.title: The number of migrant workers employed in China's construction industry in the first half of 2026 was over 15 million below the 2021 peak, according to Chinatimes, which bases its report on National Bureau of Statistics data.
item.description:
Chinatimes, citing the National Bureau of Statistics of China, reports that the total number of migrant workers rose 0.1% to 295 million in 2022 and rose slightly to 297 million in 2023, with the growth rate slowing again, and that in 2024 the share of migrant workers working outside their home areas fell for the first time while the share of local employment rose significantly. It states that in the first half of 2026 the number of migrant workers employed in the construction industry was over 15 million lower than at the peak in 2021. The row gives no figure for the 2021 peak or for the 2026 level, no percentage change for construction and no data on construction output or floor space, so the size of the fall relative to the sector's workforce cannot be calculated from it. It is the only row in the input on this series.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a head count, not construction activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, fewer construction workers are consistent with less building activity but also with higher productivity or a shift of workers to other sectors, so the series is an indirect signal. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction uses of adhesive technologies follow the area built and renovated more closely than the number of workers; the row gives no figures on either. Points that may be worth considering include National Bureau of Statistics data on floor space started and completed and the next release of the migrant worker survey.

Chinatimes

item.title: Italy approved measures to limit the effect of rising gas prices on electricity bills for households and businesses from January, with an average cut of about EUR 15 per megawatt-hour; the state will reimburse part of the cost of gas used for power.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that Italy has approved measures to limit the impact of rising gas prices on electricity bills for households and businesses from January, according to energy minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin. The measures will result in an average reduction of about EUR 15 per megawatt-hour, and the government will reimburse a portion of the cost of natural gas used for thermoelectric power generation. The row says that Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces mounting protests over the cost of living ahead of general elections due next year, and that Italy uses gas to produce almost half of its electricity, the highest proportion in the European Union. The row does not give the total cost of the measure, how it is financed, how long it lasts, the current electricity price or which businesses qualify.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a government measure with one average figure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a subsidy that reimburses part of the cost of gas used for power lowers the price paid by buyers but not the underlying cost of gas, and its size depends on public funding. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Italian manufacturers of building materials, machinery and vehicles use electricity in their plants, so lower power prices affect their costs and their competitiveness against producers in other countries; the row gives no figure for industrial electricity prices. Points that may be worth considering include the scope for industrial users, the duration of the measure and gas price developments over the winter.

MarketScreener

item.title: FederUnacoma's president says agricultural machinery sales are falling in the main markets: US tractors down 13% in January-September, Brazil down 19% in seven months to July, Argentina down 27% in six months to June.
item.description:
FederUnacoma president Mariateresa Maschio says that sales of agricultural machinery are falling across the main markets, with inflation, the climate emergency and the crisis in farm incomes hampering sales. In the United States tractor sales fell 13% between January and September, continuing a four-year downward trend; the number of machines sold fell by over 100,000 units, from 318,000 in 2021 to 196,000 in 2025. In Canada sales fell by over 9% (the row gives no period). In Brazil tractor sales were down 19% in the seven months to July and in Argentina a 27% decline was recorded in the six months to June. In Italy, a second FederUnacoma release says the market reversed in late spring and summer, that the downturn continued into September and October, and that manufacturers' turnover is forecast to fall 4.3% in 2026 from 2025 with domestic demand and an expected contraction in exports weighing on it; it says potential demand remains high but investment support is needed. Both rows are the association's own releases and give no figures for Europe outside Italy, for China or India, or for machine types other than tractors.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows are an industry association's statements with unit figures for some markets. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling machine sales reduce the order books of machinery makers and their suppliers and push producers to cut costs. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, machinery manufacturing is one of the customer industries for adhesive technologies used in assembly and protection, so lower unit output reduces demand from it; the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the association's data for the remaining months of 2026, farm income data in the main markets and any investment support measures.

FederUnacoma | FederUnacoma

item.title: France's furniture and wood-based panel employer and union organisations presented a joint plan of ten proposals, saying the sector has lost over half its jobs in 25 years and one company in four is deemed fragile or threatened by the Banque de France.
item.description:
The French furniture craft union UNAMA reports that all employer and trade union organisations representing the furniture and wood-based panel manufacturing sector in France have come together for the first time to present a shared diagnosis and ten proposals for an emergency plan. The diagnosis says that over 50% of the sector's jobs have been destroyed in 25 years, including 2,500 in the last three years, that net profitability was 2.5% of turnover in 2024 against 4.2% in 2021, that one company in four is deemed fragile or threatened by the Banque de France against one in five on average in industry, and that company failures rose 17% over the twelve rolling months to the end of June 2026. It names three causes: a historically low real estate market, weakened household confidence that favours savings over equipment purchases, and competition deemed unfair from products imported from China, particularly via online sales platforms. The plan has three priorities: reviving consumption of furniture made in France, restoring the competitiveness of furniture manufacturing and craft, and ensuring fair competition. The row does not list the ten proposals and gives no production volumes or panel output; the figures are the sector's own diagnosis as relayed by UNAMA.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a sector's own diagnosis and requests, not a measurement by an outside body, apart from the Banque de France assessment of company fragility. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, weak housing activity lowers demand for furniture, and a sector that loses jobs and companies also loses purchases of the materials it uses. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, wood-based panels and furniture assembly are applications of adhesive technologies, so lower output in this sector reduces demand for them; the row gives no volumes of adhesives or panels. Points that may be worth considering include the government's response to the ten proposals, French housing data and the sector's failure statistics for the second half of 2026.

UNAMA

item.title: German exports rose 2.0% in September from August to EUR 141.1 billion and imports rose 4.2% to EUR 125.5 billion, so the trade surplus narrowed to EUR 15.6 billion from EUR 17.9 billion, the statistics agency reported.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports, citing Germany's statistics agency, that exports rose 2.0% on the month to EUR 141.1 billion in September while imports rose 4.2% to EUR 125.5 billion. The trade surplus narrowed to EUR 15.6 billion from EUR 17.9 billion in August and was little changed from EUR 15.5 billion a year earlier. The row says the figures follow signs of a tentative recovery in German industry, with manufacturing orders rising in September alongside industrial production, and that resilience continues to be supported by government investment in infrastructure and defence. It adds that disruptions to competitors in Asia have also given some German manufacturers a boost since the outbreak of war in the Middle East, while deeper structural shifts weigh on Germany's traditional export model, with Chinese manufacturers providing intense competition in sectors such as automobiles, machinery and industrial equipment. The row does not say whether the figures are adjusted for seasonal effects, does not split the change into price and volume, and gives no breakdown by destination or product. It is the only row in the input on these figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports trade values for one month, with no price and volume split. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a narrower surplus produced by imports growing faster than exports can reflect higher import prices or stronger domestic demand for inputs, and one month does not set a trend. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German machinery and vehicle makers are among the customers whose export orders set their demand for bonding, sealing and coating materials, and the row names Chinese competition in exactly those sectors; the row gives no figures for chemicals or materials trade. Points that may be worth considering include the October trade data, the split of exports by destination and the volume series behind the values.

MarketScreener

item.title: China's domestic passenger vehicle sales fell 27.3% year on year to 1.65 million in October while passenger vehicle exports rose 68.2% to 932,000, and car exports grew 75% in January-October, according to the China Passenger Car Association.
item.description:
Based on data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) released on 9 November, MarketScreener, The Standard, Commercial Times and Lianhe Zaobao report that domestic passenger vehicle sales were 1.65 million units in October, 27.3% below a year earlier, while passenger vehicle exports were 932,000 units, up 68.2%. Commercial Times reports that car exports rose 75% between January and October compared with the same period of 2025, Lianhe Zaobao reports that automotive exports grew 75% year on year in the first ten months of 2026, and Lianhe Zaobao calls October the 12th consecutive month of decline in domestic sales. Lianhe Zaobao reports CPCA president Cui Dongshu calling on Chinese automotive companies to accelerate the localisation of their overseas operations, keep core technologies at home, expand overseas production and promote the globalisation of Chinese standards. Bloomberg separately reports that Chinese automakers have lost USD 269 billion in market value, a 45% drop, since a peak of nearly USD 600 billion in September 2025, with BYD and Xiaomi accounting for most of it, as competition squeezes profits; market value is a different measure from sales. The rows give no production figures, no breakdown by brand or by electric and combustion vehicles, no export destinations and no cause for the fall in domestic sales.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report sales and export units, not output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, vehicles exported from China are still built in Chinese plants, so the materials they use stay tied to Chinese suppliers, while a shift to production abroad would move that demand to the new locations. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, demand follows vehicle output and model design rather than sales, and the CPCA president's call for overseas production points to assembly capacity that may be built outside China, which would change where bonding and sealing materials are bought; the rows give no production or materials figures. Points that may be worth considering include the CPCA's November data and announcements of overseas plants by Chinese carmakers.

MarketScreener | The Standard | Commercial Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Bloomberg

item.title: Brent crude fell below USD 92 a barrel on 10 November after settling 5.85% lower the previous session, its lowest since 31 August; The Economic Times links the fall to Trump saying he believes the Iran war is effectively over.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports that on 10 November oil extended its losses, falling around 6% in two days after Trump said he believes the war in Iran "is effectively over". Brent futures fell 0.88% (USD 0.81) to below USD 92 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate fell 0.91% (USD 0.79) to USD 86; Brent had settled 5.85% lower in the previous session after sliding to its lowest since 31 August. Arab News reports that on 9 November, after meeting Qatar's prime minister, Trump saw "positive momentum" toward a deal, said the war is "militarily is effectively over" and that "we're just keeping it the status quo", and wrote on Truth Social that a resumption of US strikes was "quite unlikely" because Gulf powers wanted to keep the status quo. The Economic Times describes the fall as a reaction to the statement; the row does not give the time of the settlement relative to the remarks. The rows give no agreement text, no Brent level for 9 November and no figures for physical oil supply or shipping.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a price move that the newspaper links to a statement, not to an agreement. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, crude oil and its derivatives are raw materials or energy inputs for many chemical products, so a lasting lower price would ease input costs with a delay, while a price that reacts to statements can reverse if talks stall. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many resins, solvents and additives are priced off oil-linked feedstocks and supplier price lists adjust with a lag; the rows give no figures for chemical or resin prices. Points that may be worth considering include the next Brent settlements, the Qatar mediation and any published agreement text.

The Economic Times | Arab News
